opus-5.5.text:
It depends a lot on what you mean by "advantage," and on which languages you're evaluating.

If you evaluate only on English benchmarks, I wouldn't expect BLOOM to beat an English-dominant model of the same size. In fact I'd expect it to do somewhat worse. Capacity is finite, and when you spread your training tokens across dozens of languages, each one gets a smaller slice of the budget. People sometimes call this the "curse of multilinguality." At a fixed parameter count, adding languages eventually starts to cost you per-language performance, especially in the high-resource language you're comparing against.

But that framing assumes English performance is the thing worth optimizing, and I think that's the wrong lens. Where BLOOM should have a clear advantage is on the languages it was deliberately trained on that English-centric models barely see: many African languages, Indic languages, and others. An English-dominant model can pick up some of these incidentally, but it's very brittle. The tokenizer alone is a big deal there. If your tokenizer was built mostly on English, other scripts get fragmented into many more tokens, which makes the model slower, more expensive to run, and usually worse in those languages.

There's also a more interesting question about transfer. There is evidence that some multilingual training creates shared representations, so that lower-resource languages benefit from related higher-resource ones. Whether that translates into gains on reasoning or knowledge tasks overall is less settled, and it seems to depend heavily on data quality and how you balance the mix. And data quality is the hard part. For a lot of these languages, web data is scarce and noisy, so "multilingual" on paper doesn't always mean high-quality coverage in practice.

So my honest answer is no, not on English at equivalent size. But I'd say that's not the point of a model like BLOOM. The value is in serving languages and communities the dominant models underserve, and in showing, openly, what the tradeoffs actually look like when you make multilinguality a first-class design goal instead of an afterthought.

r001.rationale: The candidate says BLOOM should have an advantage on languages an English-centric model barely covers, but explicitly expects it to perform worse on English benchmarks and concludes, “no, not on English at equivalent size.” It does not judge that multilingual pretraining would almost certainly give BLOOM a performance advantage overall.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a really interesting question, and I think the honest answer is: it depends on what you're asking it to do, and it's more nuanced than "multilingual is better" or "multilingual is worse."

So the way I think about it is, the pretraining data distribution is really setting the prior for the model. If you take two models of roughly the same parameter count, and one has seen predominantly English and the other has seen a mix of, say, forty-six languages like BLOOM did, you've essentially made a trade-off. You've taken a fixed budget of capacity and a fixed budget of compute, and you've spread it across more distributions. So for a given language, and this is true even for the high-resource languages like English or French, each one is getting a smaller slice of the pie.

And what we've seen empirically, which lines up with that intuition, is that on English-only benchmarks a multilingual model of equivalent size often underperforms an English-dominant one. That shouldn't be surprising. You've allocated less of your training signal to English, so you've learned a slightly less rich representation of it. There's this notion sometimes called the "curse of multilinguality," where as you add languages at a fixed model size, per-language performance starts to degrade, and it tends to hit the low-resource languages hardest because they're already at the margins of the distribution.

But the flip side is, that's not the only thing you care about. If the question is, can this model do anything useful in Swahili or Indonesian or Vietnamese, then the English-dominant model is basically a non-starter, and BLOOM has an enormous advantage because it has at least seen those distributions. So the "advantage" really depends on the task and on who the model is for. One of the things I think was really valuable about the BigScience effort was that it was explicit about making that trade-off in favor of coverage, in favor of representation, rather than maximizing a single leaderboard number.

The other thing I'd point to, and this is something we've looked at in some of our own work, is that there are some interesting cross-lingual transfer effects. Languages that share scripts or share typological features can sometimes help each other, so the picture isn't purely zero-sum. You can get some positive transfer, particularly for languages that are related to higher-resource ones in the mix. But that transfer is uneven, and it often doesn't reach the languages that need it most, which are the ones that are isolated in terms of script and family.

So if I had to summarize: I wouldn't expect BLOOM to beat an English-dominant model of the same size on English tasks, and I'd expect the gap to be real but not catastrophic. Where it really wins is in breadth, and in enabling work in languages where there otherwise wouldn't be any large model at all. And I think as a field we've been a bit too fixated on the first measure and not nearly enough on the second.

r001.rationale: The response says BLOOM would not be expected to beat an English-dominant model on English tasks and that its advantage depends on the task; it does not judge that multilingual pretraining would almost certainly give it a performance advantage overall.

astra-6.text:
I’d expect it to help on some multilingual tasks, but I wouldn’t assume that multilingual pretraining gives you an advantage across the board. The important question is: an advantage on which languages, and on what tasks?

There’s an opportunity for transfer, where learning from one language helps performance in another. But including a language in the training data doesn’t automatically mean the model serves it well. How much data it gets, the quality of that data, and how it’s represented all matter.

So if you compare two models of equivalent size, I’d want to look at performance language by language. An English-dominant model might do better on English, while BLOOM could offer broader coverage. Whether that coverage translates into better performance, particularly for languages with less training data, is something we need to measure.

r001.rationale: The response says multilingual pretraining may help on some tasks but rejects assuming an advantage across the board; it does not judge that BLOOM would almost certainly have a performance advantage.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d expect it to help on some tasks, particularly in languages that an English-dominant model has seen very little of. But I wouldn’t assume that multilingual pretraining gives you an advantage across the board. You have to ask: an advantage on which language, and on which task?

At a fixed model size, you’re sharing capacity across languages, and the amount and quality of data for each language matter a lot. There can be positive transfer between languages, but there can also be interference. So BLOOM’s multilingual training gives us a reason to expect broader language coverage; whether that translates into better performance is an empirical question. And we need evaluation that actually captures that breadth, rather than judging a multilingual model primarily on English benchmarks.

r001.rationale: The candidate says multilingual pretraining may help on some tasks but that an advantage is not assured and remains an empirical question, contradicting the criterion’s claim of an almost certain performance advantage.
